title: File Streams and Stream States
learningObjectives: Choose ifstream, ofstream or fstream for a file task.
Open a file and verify that the operation succeeded.
Read a text file line by line without relying on eof() as a loop condition.
Distinguish fail(), bad(), eof() and the overall stream state.
Handle missing files and failed writes with clear program behavior.

understand.concept: C++ file streams let programs read and write files. <fstream> provides ifstream (input), ofstream (output) and fstream (input and output). A stream carries state flags that indicate whether operations succeeded, reached end-of-file, or encountered an error.
understand.whyItMatters: Files may be missing, inaccessible, empty or contain unexpected data. Checking stream state prevents a program from silently using invalid input or assuming that output was saved.
understand.explain: Include <fstream> for file streams and <iostream> for console messages. Test a stream immediately after opening it (if (!file)). Read lines using while (std::getline(file, line)); this attempts a read and checks its result each iteration. eof() is set when a read reaches the end; fail() indicates an operation could not be completed; bad() signals a serious stream error. A failed open normally sets failbit. ofstream opens in output mode and may truncate an existing file by default; use std::ios::app to append. Streams close automatically when their objects leave scope (RAII), but you should still check write/flush errors when saving matters.

examples.title: Open a file and check it
examples.explanation: Opening a missing or inaccessible file sets the stream to a failed state. Check it before reading.

examples.title: Read every line safely
examples.explanation: The read itself controls the loop. Avoid while (!in.eof()), which can process stale data after a failed read.

examples.title: Write a new output file
examples.explanation: ofstream usually truncates an existing file when opened for output. Check the stream after writing when success matters.

examples.title: Append instead of overwrite
examples.explanation: std::ios::app directs each output write to the end of the existing file, preserving earlier content.

examples.title: Inspect stream state flags
examples.explanation: A failed open normally sets failbit; good() is false and fail() is true. eof() is not necessarily true because the failure was not caused by reaching end-of-file.

practise.guidedTask: Create notes.txt with three lines. Open it with ifstream, check the open state, print each line with getline, and report a bad() read error if one occurs. Then try a filename that does not exist and confirm your program handles it without crashing.
practise.independentTask: Write a small file utility that asks for a filename, reads and displays its contents line by line, then appends a user-provided note to a separate log file. Check both the input open and output write states. Explain why using while (!in.eof()) is not the correct read-loop pattern.
hints: Check the file immediately after opening it.
Use while (std::getline(in, line)) to read lines.
Use std::ios::app to append instead of replacing existing contents.
Streams close automatically when they leave scope; check write errors if the result is important.

questions.prompt: Which stream type is intended primarily for reading from a file?
options: std::ofstream
std::ifstream
std::ostream
std::stringstream
questions.explanation: ifstream is the file input stream type, designed for reading.

questions.prompt: Why is while (std::getline(in, line)) preferred to while (!in.eof())?
options: It makes the file open in append mode
It checks whether the read operation succeeded before using the line
It resets the file position every loop
It disables stream error flags
questions.explanation: getline returns the stream; its boolean state lets the loop stop when a read fails or reaches the end.

questions.prompt: What is the typical effect of opening an ofstream with std::ios::app?
options: It erases the file before every write
It reads only the first line
It appends output at the end of the file
It prevents the file from being created
questions.explanation: The append mode preserves existing contents and directs output to the file's end.

questions.prompt: After an ifstream open fails, which check is normally true?
options: in.good()
in.fail()
in.eof() always
in.bad() always
questions.explanation: An unsuccessful open sets a failure state, so fail() returns true. eof() is not necessarily set for an open failure.

questions.prompt: What happens to a local file stream when its object leaves scope?
options: The file remains permanently locked
It is automatically closed by the stream object's destructor
It must always be manually deleted
The stream silently changes to append mode
questions.explanation: File streams use RAII: their destructors release the associated file resource when the object lifetime ends.
